newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Colston capers.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Colston capers.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)

"Rebuilding a sense of trust between the elected and those who elect them is very important to me ... if I've made a bit of progress on that in a year or two I will be very pleased indeed." - Prime Minister John Howard, March 4, 1996.
Working well so far.

In the 13 months since Howard made those commitments -- in the afterglow of his runaway election victory -- the prime minister has lost two frontbenchers, Jim Short and Brian Gibson, for conflict of interest breaches. Two other Coalition figures, backbencher Michael Cobb and former frontbencher Bob Woods, are facing fraud charges.

And then there's Mal Colston, who finally appears to have become more trouble than he's worth to the Prime Minister. Not that he hadn't given good value for the money to the government ... until his "sloppy book-keeping" defence over bogus travel claims collapsed last week.
The question is whether the pain Colston is now causing the government will cause the coalition long term electoral damage.
For a relatively few shekels of silver, Colston's vote in the Senate helped deliver nearly A$7 billion in budget cuts and the part sale of Telstra. Not bad for a year's work.
But the cost has been increasing for some time. At every twist and turn in the Colston Inc saga, coalition backbenchers have been inundated with calls from angry voters.

They're not upset about Colston's interesting approach to travel claims per se. It's just -- funny people that they are -- they think all politicians are rorters and coalition backbenchers are being tarred with that brush.
It's against that additional background that Howard acted on Tuesday night to cut Colston adrift. Like all good politicians, he was attempting to turn adversity to advantage.
There was collateral damage, certainly, in the about face. Only two weeks before that, two of his senior Cabinet colleagues had gone out on a limb to support the "sloppy book-keeping" defence.

Government Senate leader Robert Hill on March 24: "... it does not prove a guilty intent at all because there is an explanation that has been given that is totally consistent with the facts that have been tabled in this place."
Not any more.

Communications Minister Richard Alston: "In other words, it is the old conspiracy theory. (Former Colston staffer) Ms Smith puts down an explanation which you do not like, so you disregard it. You say, 'clearly it is fabricated'."
Well, that's certainly what Christine Smith now says, and with sufficient credibility, according to the Prime Minister, for him to cut Colston loose.
Mrs Smith's about-face may have been a cloud for the government, but it also contained a silver lining.
It gave Howard the chance -- at last -- to separate himself from Colston.
The government's hope is that the voters will stop seeing Colston as one of the Coalition's own and hence halt the damage to its standing with the electorate.
Fronting the press gallery on Tuesday night was an uncomfortable experience for Howard, but nowhere near as painful as the effort he'd had to go through to get his hands on the Smith document.
Initial attempts to extract the three page statement from ruggedly independent Senate clerk Harry Evans proved a dismal failure and infuriated the Prime Minister.
Shades of Paul Keating who used to rail against Evans' unrepentant and aggressive independence -- eventually provoking the former Prime Minister to damn the Senate as "unrepresentative swill".
It was a statement he lived to regret and even provided fuel for Howard's election claim to aspire to higher standards.

The Prime Minister has not made Keating's mistake. Another advantage for Howard is that unless he mishandles the rest of the Colston saga, he's unlikely to be called to account over standards at the next election.
What was a key issue in 1996 will probably be a sideline murmur in 1999.
Jobs and growth are more likely to determine just how well or badly the coalition fares at the next election.

And that's just one reason Colston is likely to leave the Senate -- not just the deputy presidency -- later rather than sooner. He may have been dumped by Howard but he can't turn back to Labor for help.
The Prime Minister still keeps emphasising the need for due process -- meaning delay -- which means the Queensland independent still has reason to feel grateful to the Coalition.
That softly-softly approach makes it even more likely Colston will help drive Howard's popularly received, if marginally effective, work-for-the-dole programme through the Senate.

And it's schemes like that which the Prime Minister is hoping will see him through the next election -- even if his 1996 pledges to cut unemployment remain unrealised when voters next go to the polls.

If sleaze is an election issue,too, Labor's inaction over Colston during its years in government ensure politicians' standards will be as much of a problem for the ALP as it would be for the Coalition.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
